overview: This file concerns Japanese colonial Taiwan’s 1939–1940 subsidy system for tea exports to the United States and other markets. American Consul Gerald Warner reports that levies on tea shipped to Manchukuo and China, supplemented by the Taiwan Government General, financed nominal advertising allowances for exporters serving third countries; he provides a firm-by-firm table of subsidies and shipment weights and warns that the payments could give Taiwan tea a price advantage. A Department of State reply records consultations with the Customs Bureau, concludes that countervailing-duty provisions did not cover duty-free tea and that no other American customs law appeared to prohibit the subsidy, and asks the consulate to monitor further developments.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Gerald Warner on subsidies for Taiwan tea exports
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the financing, allocation, commercial effects, and possible legal implications of subsidies paid on Taiwan tea shipped to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Warner explains that high tea prices generated by demand in Manchukuo led the Japanese authorities to impose levies on shipments to Manchukuo and China and use the proceeds to support exports to third countries. After Acting Commissioner of Customs Frank Shaw advised that duty-free tea was not subject to countervailing duties under section 303 of the Tariff Act of 1930, American and British exporters sought a share of the assistance. The despatch gives a detailed table distributing ¥335,975.34 among fifteen exporters on 7,420,000 kin of tea, with additional money reserved for advertising at the New York World's Fair. Warner notes that the grants were not necessarily spent on advertising, describes a new invoice declaration required by the consulate, and asks whether other American regulations apply to subsidized duty-free imports.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply on the legality of subsidized duty-free tea
subfiles.from: Henry F. Grady, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Conveys the Department’s conclusion that the Taiwan tea subsidy did not appear to violate American customs law and requests continuing reports.
subfiles.summary: State found countervailing duties applied only to dutiable goods, not duty-free tea, and saw no other customs violation or likely Anti-Dumping Act case; no consular action was needed beyond reporting developments in the subsidy's administration.

interest: Shows Japan subsidizing Taiwan tea exports via Manchukuo/China trade revenue, escaping U.S. countervailing duties.
